newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden seeks low nickel content in euro coins.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seeks low nickel content in euro coins.

text.p: Sweden pressed its case on Monday for having as little nickel as possible in the EU's euro coins, arguing the metal could cause health problems.
European Union finance ministers postponed a decision on the sensitive issue.
They also discussed whether the new single currency coins should be multi-sided, but agreed to wait for proposals from the European Commission.
"There are a few technical questions outstanding," Dutch Finance Minister Gerrit Zalm, who chaired the meeting, told a news conference.
The euro coins are due to enter circulation in 2002 in countries participating in economic and monetary union (EMU).
Sweden says nickel can cause allergies and wants as little as possible in the coins and vending machine operators have expressed concern about the effect of multi-sided coins on their business.
To help blind people tell one coin from another, an expert group had suggested making it seven-sided.
Diplomats said it would be some months before the Commission came up with proposals.
Asbrink said Sweden could not accept a decision which meant that there would be a lot of nickel in the new coins.
"This is an important question for Sweden," he told a press conference, adding he believed several countries would show understanding for Stockholm's position.
But, he added, "there is no doubt that there is a varying degree of awareness about the health problems...I am convinced that time is on our side."
Asbrink also said Sweden had shown that there was a good alternative in the country's 10-crown coin which instead of nickel used a metal mix called "Nordic gold", consisting mainly of copper.
